subjective.question: What are the main features of contemporary globalization?
subjective.answer: Contemporary globalization is the present-day phase of worldwide integration, driven above all by the revolution in information and communication technologies. Its main features are: (1) a rapid increase in international trade and cross-border investment, dominated by transnational corporations; (2) fast, large-scale global flows of finance and capital; (3) instant worldwide communication through satellite television, mobile phones and the internet, which has compressed time and space; (4) global media and cultural flows, so that the same films, news and brands reach audiences everywhere; (5) a growing role of international organizations such as the WTO, IMF and World Bank; (6) increased migration and movement of people; and (7) growing global interdependence, in which an event in one part of the world immediately affects all others.

subjective.question: What do you understand from the phrase 'one globe, many worlds'?
subjective.answer: The phrase means that humanity shares a single planet - one globe - yet lives in many separate 'worlds' at the same time. These worlds are the different nations, cultures, religions, languages, levels of development and political systems into which humankind remains divided. Globalization is linking the one globe together through trade, media, technology and travel, but it has not merged the many worlds into one: a villager in Pakistan, a banker in New York and a farmer in Africa inhabit the same planet but experience very different social, cultural and economic realities. The phrase therefore underlines both the unity created by globalization and the diversity and inequality that still persist within it.

subjective.question: Define globalization and discuss its main dimensions.
subjective.answer: Globalization is the process of growing interaction, integration and interdependence among the people, companies and governments of different nations, driven by international trade, investment and information technology. Its main dimensions are: (1) Economic - global markets, trade, finance and transnational corporations; (2) Political - international organizations, global governance and cross-border political cooperation; (3) Cultural - worldwide flow of media, ideas, values and lifestyles; (4) Technological - instant communication and transport that shrink distance; and (5) Social - migration, tourism and people-to-people contact across borders.

subjective.question: What is meant by globalization of media? Discuss its main drivers.
subjective.answer: Globalization of media means the worldwide production, distribution and consumption of media content across national boundaries, so that news, films, television programmes and music circulate globally rather than remaining within one country. Its main drivers are: (1) satellite and cable technology, which carry channels across continents; (2) the internet and digital technology, which make content instantly available everywhere; (3) large transnational media conglomerates that own outlets in many countries; (4) deregulation and privatization of media in most countries since the 1980s and 1990s; and (5) global advertising, which finances content aimed at worldwide audiences.

subjective.question: Explain Marshall McLuhan's concept of the 'global village'.
subjective.answer: The Canadian scholar Marshall McLuhan proposed that electronic media - first television and later digital networks - have shrunk the world into a 'global village'. Because electronic communication is instantaneous, events anywhere on Earth can be seen and felt everywhere at the same time, just as news spreads by word of mouth in a small village. People across the world therefore share experiences, react together and become interdependent like the residents of one village. McLuhan also argued that 'the medium is the message': the medium of communication itself shapes society and human perception more deeply than the content it carries.

subjective.question: What is cultural imperialism? How do global media contribute to it?
subjective.answer: Cultural imperialism is the domination of the culture of a weaker society by that of a powerful one, usually through the one-way flow of media content. Critics such as Herbert Schiller argue that global media are owned mainly by Western, especially American, conglomerates, so films, television programmes, news and advertising carry Western values, lifestyles and consumer culture into developing countries. This one-way flow can weaken local cultures, languages and media industries, create dependence on foreign content and shape the tastes and thinking of audiences in the developing world in favour of the dominant culture and its products.

subjective.question: What is the difference between globalization and internationalization?
subjective.answer: Internationalization refers to increasing relations and exchanges between nation-states - such as trade or diplomacy - while the states themselves remain separate and fully in control. Globalization is a deeper process: it involves integration that goes beyond and weakens national boundaries, through global markets, transnational companies, worldwide media and instant communication, so that decisions and events in one country are shaped by forces operating at the global level. In short, internationalization is cooperation between distinct nations, whereas globalization is the emergence of a single interconnected global system.

subjective.question: Discuss the positive and negative effects of media globalization on local cultures.
subjective.answer: Positive effects: global media give local audiences access to world news, education, entertainment and diverse viewpoints; they spread awareness of health, rights and development issues; they allow local cultures and diasporas to reach global audiences; and competition from foreign channels improves the quality of local media. Negative effects: the dominance of foreign, especially Western, content can erode local languages, dress, values and traditions; imported consumer culture promotes materialism; local film and television industries struggle against the cheap, polished products of big conglomerates; and unsuitable foreign content may conflict with local religious and social norms. The overall impact therefore depends on how a society regulates, adapts and responds to global media.

subjective.question: Name the major global media conglomerates and explain how they influence world media flows.
subjective.answer: A small number of transnational conglomerates - such as Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery, Comcast (NBCUniversal), Paramount, News Corporation and Bertelsmann - own film studios, television networks, publishing houses and digital platforms across many countries. Together with global news agencies such as Reuters, the Associated Press and AFP, they dominate the production and distribution of the world's entertainment and news. Because most media content flows from these few companies in the developed West to the rest of the world, they exercise great influence over what the world watches, what is treated as important news and which values and lifestyles are presented as normal and desirable.

subjective.question: What are the main elements of the political system of Pakistan?
subjective.answer: The political system of Pakistan rests on the Constitution of 1973, which declares Pakistan a federal, parliamentary Islamic republic. Its main elements are: (1) the Constitution, the supreme law defining rights, institutions and the Islamic character of the state; (2) the Parliament (Majlis-e-Shoora), consisting of the National Assembly and the Senate, which makes laws; (3) the executive - the President as head of state and the Prime Minister and cabinet, who hold real executive power; (4) an independent judiciary headed by the Supreme Court, with High Courts in the provinces; (5) the federal structure, dividing powers between the federation and the four provinces; (6) political parties and an electoral system based on adult franchise, supervised by the Election Commission; (7) the civil and military bureaucracy, which administers the state and has historically played a significant political role; and (8) supporting elements such as the media, local governments and civil society, which influence and check the working of the system.

subjective.question: 'Politics is the process by which power should be used for the benefit of the people.' Discuss.
subjective.answer: Politics is the process through which power in a society is acquired, organized and exercised. The statement presents the ideal, democratic view of politics: power is not an end in itself and does not belong to rulers for their personal benefit; it is a trust that must be used for the welfare of the people. In this sense, genuine politics means making decisions, laws and policies that serve the public interest - providing security, justice, education, health and economic opportunity. Where power is used for self-enrichment or oppression, politics degenerates into exploitation. The statement therefore sets the standard by which political leadership should be judged: the benefit of the people.

subjective.question: Discuss any three types of issues that result into political grouping.
subjective.answer: Political groupings and parties form when people unite around shared issues. Three main types of issues produce such grouping are: (1) Ethnic and linguistic issues - people group together on the basis of language, tribe, caste or regional identity, demanding recognition, resources or autonomy for their group; (2) Religious and sectarian issues - differences of religion, sect and interpretation of the role of religion in the state bring people together into religious parties and movements; and (3) Economic and class issues - the conflicting interests of landlords, industrialists, traders, workers and peasants over land, wages, taxes and prices produce class-based political groupings. Ideological and provincial issues may reinforce these basic divisions.

subjective.question: What are the main components of the information sector of Pakistan?
subjective.answer: The information sector covers all the organized means by which information and content are produced and delivered in the country. Its main components are: (1) the print media - newspapers, magazines and periodicals; (2) the electronic media - television and radio, both state-owned (PTV, Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation) and private channels; (3) news agencies, such as the Associated Press of Pakistan (APP); (4) the advertising industry, which finances most media; (5) public relations and corporate communication; (6) the film industry and other entertainment production; (7) book publishing and printing; (8) telecommunications - telephone, mobile and internet services - which carry information; and (9) information technology and postal and courier services. The mass media are thus only one part of a much wider information sector.

subjective.question: What do you understand by historical nation-states? Also give examples.
subjective.answer: Historical nation-states are states that emerged gradually through a long historical process, in which a people sharing a common language, culture, territory and historical experience developed into a nation and then acquired their own state. They were not created suddenly by an outside power. Examples include France, England (Britain), Japan, China, Egypt and Iran (Persia), whose national identities evolved over many centuries. They are usually contrasted with post-colonial nation-states, such as Pakistan, India, Iraq and Nigeria, which were created at the end of colonial rule, often within boundaries drawn by the departing colonial power.

subjective.question: Jot down the main postulates of the Pakistan Population Policy 2002.
subjective.answer: The main postulates (objectives) of the Pakistan Population Policy 2002 are: (1) to reduce the population growth rate to 1.3 percent by the year 2020; (2) to reduce the total fertility rate to the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman by 2020; (3) to increase the use of contraception and meet the unmet need for family planning services; (4) to make reproductive health and family planning services universally available and accessible, especially in rural areas; (5) to involve NGOs, the private sector and other government departments, not only the Population Welfare Programme, in delivering services; (6) to promote the small-family norm through information, education and communication; and (7) to address related issues such as infant and maternal mortality, female education and the empowerment of women, so that population stabilization supports national development.

subjective.question: What are the different scales or levels of NGOs?
subjective.answer: NGOs operate at different scales or levels according to the area and community they serve: (1) Local or community level - small community-based organizations (CBOs) working in a village, neighbourhood or town on local problems such as water, sanitation and basic education; (2) Provincial or regional level - organizations working across a district or province, coordinating many local groups; (3) National level - large NGOs operating all over the country, such as the Edhi Foundation or the Aga Khan development network organizations in Pakistan, with professional staff and nationwide programmes; and (4) International level - INGOs such as Oxfam, Save the Children and the Red Cross/Red Crescent, which work in many countries, raise funds globally and usually operate through national or local partners. As the level rises, the size, funding, professionalization and area of operation of the NGO increase.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a nation, a state and a nation-state.
subjective.answer: A nation is a community of people bound together by a shared language, culture, history, territory and a sense of common identity and belonging; it is primarily a cultural and psychological bond. A state is a political and legal organization: a defined territory, a permanent population, an organized government and sovereignty, recognized by other states. A nation-state is a state whose population largely consists of a single nation, so that the political unit and the national unit coincide - for example, Japan or France. Many modern states are multi-national states rather than nation-states, because several nations live within their borders.

subjective.question: What is a multi-national state? Give examples.
subjective.answer: A multi-national state is a single sovereign state within whose borders two or more distinct nations - peoples with their own languages, cultures and identities - live together. Pakistan is a multi-national state because Punjabis, Sindhis, Pashtuns, Baloch, Seraiki-speaking people, Mohajirs and others, each with a distinct language and culture, are citizens of one state. Other examples are Switzerland, where German, French, Italian and Romansh speakers form one state, India, Canada and the former Soviet Union. Such states usually adopt a federal system and must manage the competing demands of their constituent nations carefully to preserve unity.

subjective.question: What is meant by post-colonial nation-states? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Post-colonial nation-states are the states that came into existence when European colonial empires withdrew from Asia and Africa, mainly after the Second World War. Their boundaries were usually those drawn by the colonial power, so they often contained several ethnic and linguistic groups, and they inherited colonial administrative structures, economies and problems of national integration. Examples include Pakistan and India (1947), Iraq, Nigeria, Kenya and Indonesia. Unlike historical nation-states, which evolved slowly over centuries, post-colonial states had to build national unity, institutions and development within a short period after independence.

subjective.question: Discuss the role of PEMRA in regulating electronic media in Pakistan.
subjective.answer: The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA), established under the PEMRA Ordinance 2002, is the regulator of private electronic media in Pakistan. Its role is to: (1) issue licences for private television channels, FM radio stations, cable television and other electronic media; (2) set and enforce a code of conduct and programme standards for licensees; (3) regulate the distribution of foreign channels and content; (4) take action - warnings, fines or suspension - against channels that violate licence conditions; and (5) expand and modernize the electronic media sector while protecting viewers' interests. PEMRA's creation ended the state monopoly over television and radio and opened the sector to private broadcasters.

subjective.question: Write a note on the development of television in Pakistan.
subjective.answer: Television came to Pakistan when Pakistan Television (PTV) began its first transmission from Lahore on 26 November 1964, as a state-owned service; a Karachi station followed, and PTV gradually covered the whole country. For decades PTV remained the only channel, joined by the semi-private STN in the 1990s. The turning point came in 2002, when PEMRA began licensing private channels; within a few years dozens of Pakistani news and entertainment channels - such as Geo, ARY, Express, Dunya and Hum - were on air through cable and satellite, transforming news coverage, entertainment and public debate in the country.

subjective.question: What is an NGO? Discuss the role of NGOs in Pakistani society.
subjective.answer: An NGO (non-governmental organization) is a voluntary, non-profit body, independent of government, that works for social welfare and development; NGOs are also known as NPOs (non-profit organizations). In Pakistan, NGOs play an important role where the state is weak: they provide health care, education, clean water, micro-credit and relief in disasters; they work for the rights of women, children and minorities; they mobilize communities and create awareness; and they supplement government development programmes, especially in rural and poor urban areas. Well-known examples include the Edhi Foundation's welfare network and rural support programmes that organize village communities for development.

subjective.question: Discuss the main features of Pakistan's National Environment Policy 2005.
subjective.answer: The National Environment Policy 2005 was Pakistan's first comprehensive national environment policy since independence. It provides a framework for addressing environmental problems while sustaining economic growth. Its main features are: conservation and sustainable management of water resources; energy efficiency and promotion of renewable energy; conservation of forests, biodiversity and natural resources; control of air and water pollution and safe management of waste; sustainable agriculture and livestock practices; and integration of environmental concerns into development planning, together with public awareness and participation. Primary education is not part of the environment policy; the policy concentrates on the protection and management of the natural environment and resources.
